## 2. Films for someone who has been stuck in hypoarousal/freeze for years and is not really living at all?

**Score:** 29
**Body:** I like slow cinema. I just want something that isn’t aggressively cheerful but shows someone deciding to live, or someone coming out of their shell for the first time. Someone who is maybe agoraphobic or afraid to be truly seen by other people and thus isolated and does the bare minimum to survive, and then they start to get better (ideally)

I only talk to my boyfriend and a work friend, all I do is watch tv, play video games. It’s actually a step up from what i used to do, which is scroll all day. I experienced some (film-worthy) trauma about a year ago, but I’ve been like this for a few years. It is kind of breaking my heart that I’m 30 and I’m not sure I’ve ever really lived. I feel like a passive observer/critic of human life. Sorry for the therapy dump, I just want to give more information so y’all can understand where I’m at and what I’m needing to see/feel. Thanks for reading

## 2. Wildwood flopping at the box office is painful

**Score:** 250
**Body:** I never expected Wildwood to be a box office success considering Laika’s track record but a small part of me really hoped it would take off with word of mouth. 

I watched it yesterday and it’s incredible from a technical perspective and a film as a whole. To some extent it may be too early to really call it a flop considering it’s week 2 but as it stands I don’t believe it’ll push forward to higher numbers.

Money isn’t everything per se, especially with this studio, but it does show where people’s interest lie and it certainly isn’t in this one. Anyway, if you haven’t seen it I believe this is the last weekend it’s in IMAX and I recommend watching it on the largest screen you possibly can.

2. I imagine it will get a second wind once academy awards nominations come out. The word on the street is that this one could win best animated picture. 
  - There's no reason it shouldn't get nominated for Best Picture. The existence of a Best Animated category has been necessary, yet it also is in itself a snub.

The other was *taken out of the theater* around the time the war began and a dagger went into a coyote's forehead. I kid you not. Took the kid right out ***at that point of the film*** and not before**.**

Beyond that, no kids were in the theater. It was all adults. It definitely isn't a "Disney-Feel-Good" movie for kids. It was gritting and had some dark elements. 

Eliminate the families from watching, and you're not going to get a lot of people unless you make something like Joker or Deadpool.

**Score:** 48
**Body:** I am still in shambles. This movie, while many think of it as pretentious eat the rich propaganda hit very personal. 

Ibelieve it understood something, that, if you have not worked in this branche, you will never feel. 

I think it only hitted so much, because i have been there. Still am. Hospitality is an industrie than can wear you down like no other. 

The strife for perfection. To please people you will never know and who not care for you. The ambition to beat everyone and be better than the others. The pressure who is putting you in the ground and will force you into dependence.

# Top 5 posts from r/TrueFilm day

## 1. Rewatching Alejandro Iñárritu’s "Babel" 20 years later, the movie feels richer than I remember

**Score:** 18
**Body:** I sided with the detractors back in the day. I saw nothing but an interlocking global drama filled with characters who behave stupidly, situations that escalate beyond plausibility, and a reductive, simplistic message along the lines of “we are all human despite our differences.”

The funny thing is, I can totally understand why that was my assessment of the movie. The characters do make dumb decisions, their predicaments escalate to improbable heights, and that plain, simple message is readily available to us. But this time around, I discovered a richer movie, with much more going on between the lines.

There’s a sharp observation on cultural baggage underlying the character’s actions that kickstart the different plots. The stories here aren’t simply about a multiplicity of languages but about incompatible systems of meaning: no one enters another culture as a blank slate; every character brings with them a set of assumptions about language, safety, authority, comfort, religion, class, and proper behavior.

We see this clearly in the Moroccan storyline that open the movie: two boys were living their ordinary rural lives when an object and people from completely different worlds enter theirs. The object is a rifle, and this rifle changes meaning depending on who encounters it. It begins as a gift from a Japanese tourist, becomes a practical tool for the Moroccan father to protect its livestock, then becomes something the boys experiment with almost as a toy.

The people are a group of Americans in a tour bus. One of them, played by Cate Blanchett, is hit by one of bullets fired from the rifle by the boys. Then, the rifle is also interpreted through an entirely different cultural and political framework: American authorities suspect terrorism, the Moroccan government gets defensive.

The tourists, all foreigners to the boys’ reality, become increasingly angry about being stranded in the nearby village — but not primarily because of security concerns. They are mostly bothered by the heat, because air conditioning is part of the standard of comfort they carry with them, and a luxury unavailable to the people who actually live in the “picturesque” pasture they chose to visit.

Every storyline here can be interpreted this way: not as a universal tale about suffering, but as an exploration of what happens when we mistake our own cultural and personal baggage for something universal.

Amelia’s storyline makes the same point through the U.S.–Mexico border. She has spent years caring for the American children and clearly loves them; within the family’s private world, she is a trusted caregiver and almost a maternal figure. But when she takes them across the border to attend her son’s wedding, she brings that understanding of her relationship with them into a system that does not recognize it in the same way.

And finally, the movie doesn’t even need to cross a national border to get the point across. The Japanese plot features Chieko, a teenage girl sharing a home, a culture, and a loss with her father; yet the two cannot fully communicate across the distances created by grief, generational expectations, and different ways of expressing emotion.

Chieko also happens to be deaf, so her isolation from the hearing world turns Tokyo into an overwhelming landscape of visual stimulation. She moves between the restraint and tradition of her home life and the hypermodernity of the world outside, while never feeling entirely at home in either.

I still don’t think this is a flawless movie. It can be heavy-handed, contrived, and almost aggressively tragic. But 20 years later, those flaws bother me less because I no longer see the film as simply saying that suffering makes us all the same. Now, I saw it as a tale about how differently we interpret the world and how misguided we are when we try to make sense of our POV as universal.

## 2. What Have You Been Watching? (Week of (November 01, 2026)

**Score:** 12
**Body:**  Please don't downvote opinions. Only downvote comments that don't contribute anything. Check out the [WHYBW archives](https://www.reddit.com/r/TrueFilm/wiki/index#wiki_what_have_you_been_watching.3F).

I was able to see this remaster in theaters on Halloween as part of Denver’s Film Fest. Theater was packed, lots of costumes including priests and nuns. Still not sure what to make of it but it was definitely interesting **7/10**
2. Today I watched Wicker - so good, totally recommend.

Yesterday: I Love Boosters. Quite good. Funny in places, a bit too daft in the third act. Quite influenced by Everything Everywhere All At Once.

Thursday: Primetime. I found this a bit flat tbh.

Wednesday: Fatherland. Such a good movie.

Tuesday: Ghosts: The possession of Button House. Some funny moments but I found it overly long and convoluted.

Monday: Clayface. It's not bad at all but like I Love Boosters it gets a bit tiresomely silly in the third act.

Last Sunday: Wildwood. Really entertaining.

So I've seen what I consider to be three modern classics in the last week in Wildwood, Wicker and Fatherland. Strongly recommend catching them if you can.

I'm hoping to see the Devils next week.
3. watched mephisto after years of having it on my watchlist, one of the best looking movies ive ever seen

watched half of king kong 1933 (had to stop cuz i was in public transport) its nice
4. Finally watched The Green Knight, and really enjoyed it. I vaguely remembered it being a bit divisive, so I looked up some old discourse around it and tbh was actually pretty surprised at how negative many people were on it (especially here on reddit, critics largely seemed to love it). 

It's probably one of my favorite visual worlds presented in a film in a long time. Loads of atmosphere and it just felt "lived in", and while watching a few scenes I specifically kept being reminded of Willow for that reason. Then I came across David Lowery's AMA on here back in 2021 around the release of the film, and in the answer to one question he straight out says he was influenced by Willow for the look of the film, which was cool to get that kind of direct confirmation. 
5. Watched The Devils (1971) at my local rep theatre in a packed auditorium on Halloween eve. Immaculate vibes in the theatre and the film did not disappoint.  I can safely say I have never seen anything like it before. The next film playing was The Lost Boys and as we walked outside there was a huge lineup and plenty of folks were dressed like new wave vampires. It was awesome. I love Halloween. 
6. I drove two and a half hours just to see Digger before it left theaters. I can’t believe people actually don’t like this movie. It’s the best new film I’ve seen since The Sound Of Metal, which is my favorite of the past decade. I really hope it comes out again for awards season. Makes me sad that so many people missed it. 

Minority Report from 2002. This era of Spielberg is really creepy and grotesque, and I find it unsettling. The depictions of human beings fall into an uncanny valley with bizarre behaviors and character choices, especially the female characters who seem almost programmatic in their speech. The cinematography, lighting, and art design suggest the world of the film is a simulation and the behaviors of the humans feel false and kind of robotic, aside from those of the main character John and his wife, who seem fully human in a way no one else quite does. It made me feel icky and the ick hasn’t worn off. 
7. Ended off a busy October with:

Blue Collar (1978)- an interesting look into blue collar/ union America. Well acted, a great screenplay, and a sad, yet realistic, ending. 

Monster House (2006)- I don’t do true horror movies so this is right up my alley. What’s interesting is that it’s not dumbed down like a lot of kids/ preteen movies can be. It’s got sharp dialogue, an interesting story, great voice acting, and the camera shots are well thought out. 

Body Heat (1981)- sexy, smart, sweltering.

## 3. Resemblances in The Master.

**Score:** 0
**Body:** I'd like to discuss the throughline of resemblances in The Master and how that factors into the themes of the film. I don't have a solid interpretation nor have I prepared every possible example, I'm more looking to provoke a discussion about it.

Two of the most prominent moments of resemblance in the film are Freddy saying the farmer looks like his father then proceeding to poison him, and Freddy saying "oh yeah, I can see the resemblance" to Val when he's introduced as Lancaster's son.

I also noticed how the man Freddy assaults at the shopping mall looks a decent amount like Lancaster Dodd. I always interpreted that moment as Freddy just taking his anger out on a random person, but maybe this moment is meant to poke at the possibility that maybe Lancaster's theory of reincarnation has some truth to it. (Not that PTA actually believes this, but that he finds it thematically interesting)

Maybe Freddy and Lancaster have known each other in many past lives, and while Freddy may not consciously know why, he feels some aggression towards this man that looks like Lancaster. Or, maybe the film is actually telling this sequence out of order, and this actually takes place after the other events in the film.

Either way it seems to be playing with time and with the echoes of a person's presence being projected through the past, present, and future.

There's also a throughline of red headed women throughout the film, Dodd's daughter in particular looks a lot like Freddy's old girlfriend.

What do you think? Are there any resemblances I'm missing?

## 4. You Can See Everything and you can spin anything

**Score:** 0
**Body:** I feel that You Can See Everything is an artistic achievement that has some elements of propaganda so it got me thinking about similar films of the past 111 years, specifically films with artistic merit that have been accused of generating undue sympathy for criminals.

🎦 THE BIRTH OF A NATION (1915)

Griffith’s film is still considered a technical achievement, with action scenes and close ups used in new ways to move the story forward. It was the first to use accelerating cuts between parallel scenes to ratchet up tension (which is still Christopher Nolan’s favorite editing technique). Portraying the 1870s Ku Klux Klan, the film reimagined them as heroes protecting innocent white damsels from brutish black men. The Klan were clearly terrorists and the dishonest portrayal in the film was designed to help the segregationist movement. The film’s release led to a resurgence of the Klan. On my personal propagandameter, this scores 100.

🎦 TAXI DRIVER (1976)

Scorsese’s achievement was in vividly capturing a sense of alienation in the big city and showing the workings of the incel mindset. The antihero at the center of the film is portrayed accurately to how we understand the worst kind of incel terrorist to behave: misogynistic, lonely, grandiose, losing touch with reality, and ultimately, violent. The character is portrayed honestly and he is not made into a hero, so this film doesn’t feel like propaganda to the same degree as The Birth of a Nation. However, it does leave out some important context. While it generates sympathy for the main character by pointing to trauma from military service in Vietnam, it ignores the larger cultural issue that leaves some young men feeling entitled to control over women. I don’t think Scorsese deliberately made incel propaganda, but his film could have that effect when the conclusion of the film shows the main character celebrated by the press after his killing spree. Propagandameter: 25

🎦 YOU CAN SEE EVERYTHING (2026)

Fielder and Oppenheim combine interviews, dramatic reenactments, and filmmakers’ testimonials to recreate the disorienting sensation of unreality under the spell of a manipulator. It seems like a true achievement but not with the same impact on the medium as the other two examples. 

Instead of examining a fictional criminal, this is a look at a real-life fraudster. The film generates sympathy for Elizabeth Holmes by showing her experience as a victim of rape and coercive control, as well as her challenges being neurodivergent. However, she is definitely not portrayed as a hero and the camera is unblinking as she struggles through some of her weak justifications and fabrications. The film also calls the filmmakers’ motives into question to further muddy the waters and arrive at the central theme: the truth is unknowable because everyone is deceptive. The filmmakers discuss their difficulty determining if Holmes is conscious of her own guilt and here they leave out important context: she was recently convicted by a jury that found she was certainly conscious of her own guilt. There is a dishonesty in the portrayal in order to manufacture ambiguity in service of the theme. The filmmakers turn the camera on themselves as they dissect the meaning of Holmes’ statements, implying that deep truths can be found there. But they never adequately explain why they ignore the most useful source of truth (the court transcript and evidence).

The fact that this film portrays a real person - and an unrepentant criminal who has not yet paid her debt to society - makes the bar for accurate portrayal higher than with fictional criminals. Also, the fact that the message of the film (the truth is unknowable, the press and courts can’t be trusted) matches the messaging used by sophisticated social media campaigns from Russian troll farms adds to the propaganda factor. The fact that the film went into production soon after Holmes hired an expensive crisis PR team also adds suspicion. It is unclear to me if the filmmakers were manipulated or were willingly complicit, but the outcome is a picture that tilts toward propaganda. The deception employed by filmmakers makes this one feel closer to Birth of a Nation than Taxi Driver. My personal propagandameter: 70

I am curious how others view You Can See Everything as propaganda and how it compares to other examples.

1. I think you missed a key detail in YCSE, at least in regard to your statement about the court evidence.

## 5. You Can See Everything is 100% a Fictional Drama

**Score:** 0
**Body:** Respectfully, any of you who think of this as a documentary are being played. This is Spinal Tap was a comedy shot documentary-style. The Blair Witch Project was a horror movie shot documentary-style. YCSE is a drama shot documentary-style.

Everyone in the movie is playing a fictional version of themselves. That is the reason why they spend an inordinate amount of time on the relatively unimportant line about Holmes saying "they are playing a character I created". She is getting another turn in the limelight doing exactly that: playing a character she created. It is the hidden agenda of the whole film. It is a minor point that is made a fuss over because it is the secret linchpin of the whole endeavor.

Before rejecting this premise outright, watch the film again with a critical eye and this possibility in mind. I am not saying the whole film was scripted line by line. But I am saying each scene was loosely scripted. There was a defined narrative arc to each scene. Scripted dialogue would have been too difficult to maintain the facade among the non-actors involved.

Critically look at facts that show you the illusion they want you to see while obscuring the deeper illusion. Evans and Holmes are captured in a couple hot-mic moments. Does that seem in any way organic to you? That media-savvy folks like them wouldn't know lav mics don't deactivate just because you walked to another room? How about Evans' nude scene? Does that really seem genuine to you, that a person would invite a documentary crew to film them naked in the shower? Or even if you think that Evans is such a narcissist to do it that a documentary crew wouldn't just politely decline? That scene has NO purpose unless there is a predetermined motive to include it. How about the argument between Evans and Fielder when the latter interviewed the Theranos 2.0 scientist? Did that seem genuine to you or a performative and stilted argument? How about Seyfried's participation? Wasn't it just a little too perfect how she acted as a stand-in for a rational audience member and asked such highly specific questions that drove the narrative arc? If you would say they framed the doc around those questions, I would counter they framed the questions she asked about how they decided in advance they wanted the scene to go.

You might ask what the purpose of such a convoluted con would be. One, Fielder is a rascally imp who loves layers of self-referentiality and aiming for some meta idea over anything straightforward. There was no other reason for him to be involved except to craft a psychological rug-pull of a film as a documentary. Two, Holmes gets to muddy the waters about her sociopathy and fraud and gets another turn in the limelight in advance of a revisionist restart to her career. Three, Evans gets to take the heat off his wife's back and put it on himself. He doesn't mind coming off as a psycho if it helps the family overall. Kind of an any-press-is-good-press kind of guy. If anyone digs into the film's financials, it wouldn't surprise me if Evans and Holmes did end up getting paid for their participation. There is no ethical conflict in paying an actor to perform a fictional role.

Watch again with this premise in mind. I guarantee you will find numerous more examples that show this is a well-crafted fictional film that still unintentionally reveals its artifice at many points.​
